m1_zero_omission_notes.summary: This chapter delves into computational thinking, algorithmic puzzle solving, height-ordering logic, parity arithmetic (even/odd rules), Virahāṅka-Fibonacci sequences, cryptarithms, and magic squares.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Children stand in line. Each child calls out the count of children standing in front of them who are taller than them. Analyzing height callout sequences (e.g., 0, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 3) allows uniquely deducing or constructing relative height arrangements.

margin_notes.title: Taller-in-Front Rule
margin_notes.content: Count how many standing ahead are strictly taller.

detailed_sections.full_notes:
Parity refers to whether an integer is Even or Odd.
Rules:
1. Even + Even = Even; Odd + Odd = Even; Even + Odd = Odd.
2. Even * Anything = Even; Odd * Odd = Odd.
Representation: Any even number = 2n; Any odd number = 2n - 1 (or 2n + 1).

margin_notes.title: Loose Sheet Parity
margin_notes.content: Sum of page numbers on a loose sheet from a book (pages 2k-1 and 2k) is always ODD.

detailed_sections.full_notes: Magic Square: An n x n grid filled with distinct integers where every row, column, and diagonal has the same sum. For a 3x3 grid using numbers 1-9, magic sum = 15, and central cell must be 5. Cryptarithm: Alphabetic puzzle where letters represent distinct digits.

margin_notes.title: 3x3 Magic Square
margin_notes.content: Center must be 5; exactly 8 distinct magic squares exist by rotation/reflection.

end_exercises.question: Liswini has 50 loose sheets (100 pages printed on both sides). Can the sum of page numbers of loose sheets be 6000? Why?
end_exercises.answer: Each sheet has front page 2k-1 and back page 2k. Sum per sheet = 2k-1 + 2k = 4k - 1, which is always an ODD number. Sum of 50 odd numbers must be EVEN. Summing 50 odd numbers yields an even total. However, let us check minimum sum of first 100 pages: sum(1..100) = 100*101/2 = 5050. Any 50 sheets from a book of 100 pages has sum = 5050. If total book has more pages, sum can be 6000 provided parity and page continuity conditions hold.

end_exercises.question: How many different magic squares can be made using numbers 1 - 9?
end_exercises.answer: There are 8 different magic squares (1 standard arrangement plus its 4 rotations and 4 reflections).

qa.question: Explain the maximum callout value.
qa.answer: The maximum callout is 7, achieved by the shortest person standing at the very back of the line when all 7 people ahead are taller.

level_1_objective_1_mark.question: The first person in a line always calls out '0'. (True / False)
level_1_objective_1_mark.answer: True (Reason: There is nobody standing in front of the first person, so count of taller people ahead is 0).

level_2_short_answer_2_3_marks.question: Determine parity of: Sum of 3 odd numbers and 2 even numbers.
level_2_short_answer_2_3_marks.answer: Odd + Odd + Odd = Odd. Even + Even = Even. Total = Odd + Even = Odd.

level_3_long_answer_5_marks.question: Prove why the center square of a 3x3 magic square containing numbers 1 to 9 must be 5.
level_3_long_answer_5_marks.answer: Sum of 1..9 = 45. Total row sum = 45/3 = 15. The center cell 'x' belongs to 4 lines (row 2, col 2, diagonal 1, diagonal 2). Summing these 4 lines gives: 4*15 = 60. In this sum, every cell 1..9 is counted once, except 'x' which is counted 4 times. So 45 + 3x = 60 => 3x = 15 => x = 5. Center cell must be 5.

level_4_competency_case_study.scenario: A 2x3 grid has boxes filled with odd 'o' or even 'e' numbers to satisfy row/column parity requirements.

qa.question: If Row 1 sum must be Even, Row 2 sum Odd, Col 1 Odd, Col 2 Even, Col 3 Odd, determine valid e/o filling.
qa.answer: Row 1: [e, e, e] (sum=e). Row 2: [o, e, e] (sum=o). Check cols: Col 1 [e,o]=o; Col 2 [e,e]=e; Col 3 [e,e]=e. Adjust cell selections to match all row and column parity targets.

m7_common_pitfalls.common_error: Assuming the tallest person in line is always standing at the very front.
m7_common_pitfalls.correct_approach: The tallest person calls out '0' regardless of where they stand in line.
